newsitem.title: USA: US Senate passes bill to end reverse mortgage scam.
newsitem.headline: US Senate passes bill to end reverse mortgage scam.

text.p: The U.S. Senate passed legislation on Friday designed to put an end to reverse mortgage scams that have bilked elderly homeowners of millions of dollars by charging fees for information available for free from the federal government.
Telemarketers have preyed on the elderly by charging fees to provide information on federally insured reverse mortgages -- loans to homeowners that are not repaid until the owner dies or moves out.
Adopted by a unanimous voice vote, the bill would bar the federal government from dealing with companies charging high fees for information on reverse mortgages.
"We've got a real problem, one that on a daily basis is geting worse and worse," Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato said during the Senate debate.
The New York Republican introduced the bill April 10, while Rep Rick Lazio, also a Republican from New York, introduced an identical bill in the House of Representatives.
A spokesman for Lazio said the House version would be considered "in the near future."
Lazio is currently working on a major housing reform bill that is expected to be voted on April 30, the spokesman said.
Sen. Chris Dodd, Democrat from Connecticut, said he expected President Bill Clinton would sign the measure into law after the House approved its version of the bill.
"I know that the President strongly supports our efforts," Dodd said.

Housing Secretary Andrew Cuomo's earlier effort to quash the scams by limiting insurance on loans arranged by so-called estate-planning services was struck down April 11 by a federal judge in Washington.
In a typical transaction, a telemarketer might charge a homeowner a fee of up to $10,000, or eight to 10 percent of the amount of the reverse mortgage loan, lawmakers said.
